articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd announces new surcharges across multiple trade routes
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd has announced a series of freight rate adjustments covering shipments from Pakistan, the Middle East, Asia and Oceania to destinations in the Arabian Gulf, North America and West Africa. The measures include two Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) and a General Rate Increase/General Rate Adjustment (GRI/GRA),...
articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd has announced a series of freight rate adjustments covering shipments from Pakistan, the Middle East, Asia and Oceania to destinations in the Arabian Gulf, North America and West Africa. The measures include two Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) and a General Rate Increase/General Rate Adjustment (GRI/GRA), with implementation dates ranging from November 6 to December 1, 2026. The changes apply to different container types and trade corridors, with charges calculated either per container or per twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU). Reefer surcharge for Pakistan–Arabian Gulf shipments Hapag-Lloyd will introduce a Peak Season Surcharge of US$500 per container for refrigerated cargo moving from Karachi and Port Qasim in Pakistan to selected Arabian Gulf destinations. The surcharge applies to 20-foot reefer containers and 40-foot high-cube reefer containers, with effect from November 16 through November 30, 2026. The destinations covered are the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Oman, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar. North America rate adjustment and Tema surcharge The carrier has also announced a GRI/GRA of US$1,000 per container for shipments from the Indian Subcontinent, Pakistan and the Middle East to North America. The adjustment covers 20-foot and 40-foot dry, reefer and special containers, including high-cube equipment. It will apply to containers gated in full from December 1, 2026, and will remain in effect until further notice. Separately, Hapag-Lloyd has announced a PSS of US$400 per TEU for cargo shipped from Asia and Oceania to Tema, Ghana. This surcharge applies to all container types and takes effect for cargo loaded on board from November 6, 2026. It will remain applicable until further notice. The three announcements introduce different charges across several trade routes, with shippers advised to consult Hapag-Lloyd’s applicable tariffs for further details.

articles.body: Kuehne+Nagel has announced three senior management appointments across the United States, Germany and Southern Europe, with the changes taking effect between November 2026 and January 2027. Daniel Randig has been appointed National Manager for the United States, effective 1 November 2026. Meanwhile, Björn Traemann will take over as National Manager for Germany on 1 January 2027. Miguel Germano will also assume the position of Cluster Manager for Spain, Portugal and Malta from 1 January 2027. The appointments involve experienced executives who have held management positions across several international markets and logistics divisions. New leadership across key logistics markets Daniel Randig brings nearly three decades of experience in the logistics industry, covering sea freight, air freight, sales and general management. He joined Kuehne+Nagel in Brazil in 2001 and subsequently held positions in the United States and the Middle East. Most recently, he served as National Air Logistics Manager for the US. Randig succeeds Marcus Bennett, who will move into a new global management role within the company. Björn Traemann has worked for Kuehne+Nagel for more than 23 years. His experience includes international leadership and Sea Logistics positions across Germany, China, Singapore, the Middle East, Belgium and Luxembourg, and Vietnam. He succeeds Tobias Jerschke, who is leaving Kuehne+Nagel after more than 28 years to pursue opportunities outside the logistics industry. Meanwhile, Miguel Germano brings 18 years of international management experience with the company. He previously held leadership positions in Portugal and Turkey before becoming National Manager for Mexico, his most recent role. Germano succeeds Miguel Ambielle Fernandez, who will also assume a new global management position within Kuehne+Nagel. According to the company, the appointments form part of its approach to developing internal leadership and drawing on international market experience. The announcement did not specify any accompanying changes to Kuehne+Nagel’s freight forwarding services or operational network.

US Central Command/Handout via REUTERS CAIRO, Nov 8 (Reuters) – Iranian media suggested explosions in southern Iran on Saturday evening were related to Iranian military activities rather than US strikes while both sides reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory following blasts heard in several areas, including on Qeshm Island in the strait. President Donald Trump had hinted at renewing major attacks on Iran after last week’s US midterm elections but there has been no sign of a large-scale US military operation, which Iran has said it would respond to by striking US and Israeli targets. Read Also: Trump’s Election Defeat Leaves Iran War With No Easy Exit Both sides have continued strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, however, restricting exports of energy and other commodities vital to the world economy. Iran’s state television said the evening explosions might be related to Iranian military activity in the waterway, where Iran said two vessels had hit mines and a third had caught fire. The US said its air force had disabled a vessel in the Gulf of Oman beyond the strait. Tasnim news agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage. Neither Iran nor the US has commented on that report. Washington said on November 2 that it had struck the island in a limited defensive measure against Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets. US AND IRAN BOTH SAY THEY STRUCK SHIPS Since the US and Israel began attacks on Iran in February, Tehran has sought the upper hand by hitting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz to block Gulf energy exports, while US forces began blockading movements to and from Iranian ports in April. The US military said on Saturday evening that its air force had fired at the stern of a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, disabling it as it tried to get through the blockade. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said two oil tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to pass through an “unauthorized route” in the Strait of Hormuz. A third tanker had also suffered an explosion and caught fire, the semi-official Fars news agency reported later. Reuters was not able to confirm any of the reported strikes. Monitors from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a bulk carrier and military forces were involved in an incident in the Gulf of Oman, approximately 18 nautical miles east of the United Arab Emirates’ city of Khor Fakkan, with damage unknown. It was unclear if it was related to the reported US attack. SAUDI STATE OIL COMPANY DAMAGED BY FALLING DEBRIS A conflict between Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia has escalated this month, enlarging the wider Middle East war. On Sunday, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said an administrative building belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco in Riyadh had been damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries or fatalities reported. Qatar , which has been mediating in talks to try to end the conflict that has shaken the world economy, on Saturday denied reports that the US and Iran had failed to reach a deal. The Qatari prime minister had affirmed that both sides were continuing ?to ?work toward an agreement, it said. Iran has submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday, saying the US was reviewing it but discussions would depend on Washington first meeting Tehran’s seven demands. These include sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and war reparations, while Washington insists nuclear issues must feature in initial talks. On Saturday, the US military said it was launching a task force to crack down on the movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material to Iran via its land borders and the Caspian Sea – part of economic measures to try to pressure Tehran. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards dismissed the plan as “wordplay,” saying it would not work because Tehran had made preparations and communicated closely with its neighbors. Misr Fertilizers Production Company MFPC.CA said it had been told of the reduction, which follows an earlier 20% cut to gas supplies for fertilizer plants. By Lucia Kassai, Devika Krishna Kumar, Charles Gorrivan and Archie Hunter Nov 8, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Oil traders are seeking approval from the US government to use some tankers that were sanctioned for their involvement in shipping illicit oil, in an effort to address a vessel crunch and lower prices. At least four companies, including Trafigura Group, Vitol Group, Mercuria Energy Group Ltd., and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. are in discussions with US officials for licenses that would allow them to purchase or lease some ships that are blacklisted by the US government, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The move comes as the Trump administration tries to lower oil prices that spiked after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, triggering the worst supply disruption in history. Freight rates, a major component in the final price of oil, surged to a record in recent weeks amid tanker shortages and the risks of sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. Ships have been forced to take on longer voyages to secure supplies and charterers have been forced to cough up higher insurance fees. Last month, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the administration is working with investors who buy idled sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use the ships to transport non-sanctioned oil. The idea is to convert “ dark tankers to legitimate tankers ,” he said. Treasury officials are reviewing applications and may issue authorizations on a case-by-case basis, rather than a blanket exemption, said the people, asking not to be named discussing private information. The talks cover about 50 of the roughly 1,600 ships currently sanctioned by the US . No decision is final and the timeframe for approvals is unclear, the people added. Representatives for ADNOC, Trafigura, Mercuria and Vitol declined to comment. The applications include supertankers, the oil industry’s largest vessels, able to transport 2 million barrels, some of the people said. The cost to send US oil to Asia in a supertanker climbed to nearly $40 a barrel in early October, up from $5, a year earlier. While rates have since softened, they remain near historical highs, contributing to oil prices that are hovering around $100 a barrel. To be sure, any licenses from the US Treasury or the Office of Foreign Assets Control would only apply to vessels sanctioned by the US. The European Union and the UK have imposed significant restrictions on Russian and Iranian oil, and targeted the so-called “shadow fleet” used to circumvent restrictions on Russian energy exports. It’s also unclear how much the measure would ultimately lower prices. The Trump administration has unleashed a series of measures aimed at lowering soaring energy costs for American consumers, including releasing millions of barrels from emergency reserves and waiving some fuel-related laws. Still, pump prices remain stubbornly elevated and were a major contributing factor to the Republican Party’s staggering losses in the midterm elections this week. The effectiveness at lowering prices will also depend on the profile of the ships rehabilitated. Repurposing tankers that had been previously idled — such as the tanker named Skipper , which has been sitting off the coast of Texas since December — would have a greater impact than just changing the status of vessels operating in the dark fleet, one of the people said. Related Article: U.S. Seizure of Shadow Fleet Tanker ‘Skipper’ Ends Years-Long Sanctions-Evasion Run While most of the sanctioned ships are older than the mainstream fleet, raising concerns about maintenance and safety, they could still be used in short-distance trips such as between the US and the Caribbean or Latin America, freeing newer tankers for long-haul voyages, the person said. The challenge for the Trump administration is to boost shipping capacity and lower oil prices while trying to prevent bad actors from get an influx of cash. As of Nov. 4, there are 1,568 ships hit by US sanctions, including 462 crude oil tankers, according to Treasury data compiled by Bloomberg. Most remain under the radar of enforcement authorities, typically switching off their satellite location signals. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Ellerman integrates Viasea into European shortsea network
articles.summary: Ellerman City Liners has integrated Viasea Shipping into its European shortsea operations, bringing the two companies under a unified operational framework. articles.body: Ellerman City Liners has integrated Viasea Shipping into its European shortsea operations, bringing the two companies under a unified operational framework. The move follows Ellerman’s acquisition of the Norwegian shortsea operator from ColliCare Holding in November 2025. Since then, the companies have worked to align their operations, schedules and customer services. The combined network connects the United Kingdom, Norway, the Netherlands, Poland and Lithuania with other European markets. It is supported by rail, road and inland transport services across Northern Europe. Ellerman said customers will gain access to coordinated schedules, aligned operating systems and a wider range of multimodal transport options through a single provider. Integration expands multimodal coverage The integration is intended to provide greater schedule flexibility and improve resilience across Ellerman’s shortsea network. It also strengthens connections between European ports and inland destinations. “Over the past months, our teams have worked closely to align operations, strengthen our service offering and ensure continuity for customers,” said Gary Cobbing, Chief Executive Officer of Ellerman City. “By combining our networks, expertise and local market knowledge, we are creating a more connected shortsea solution that supports customers with reliable, efficient and sustainable door-to-door transport options across Europe,” he added. Ellerman said the unified organisation will continue developing alternatives to long-distance road freight by combining shortsea shipping with rail and road transport. The company operates as part of the wider GB Global network.

articles.title: Cavotec reports record order backlog as Q3 revenue rises
articles.summary: Cavotec reported a record order backlog of €160 million at the end of September 2026, supported by growing demand for shore power systems and motorised cable reels across the maritime, ports and industrial sectors. articles.body: Cavotec reported a record order backlog of €160 million at the end of September 2026, supported by growing demand for shore power systems and motorised cable reels across the maritime, ports and industrial sectors. The engineering company’s third-quarter revenue increased by 18.9% to €42.6 million, compared with €35.8 million in the corresponding period of 2025. Order intake rose by 28.8% to €46.8 million, while operating earnings (EBIT) improved to €0.8 million from a loss of €0.5 million a year earlier. Adjusted EBIT reached €1 million, compared with a loss of €0.2 million in the third quarter of 2025. Operating cash flow also increased to €7.8 million from €2.8 million. Despite these improvements, Cavotec reported a quarterly net loss of €1.6 million, slightly lower than the €1.7 million loss recorded a year earlier. Shore power demand supports order growth Cavotec attributed its stronger quarterly performance primarily to higher demand for shore power equipment and motorised cable reels, particularly within the port and mining industries. The company’s order backlog reached an all-time high of €160 million, representing an increase of 27.2% compared with the corresponding period of 2025. During the third quarter, Cavotec secured an order worth approximately €8 million to supply shore power systems for newbuild container ships operated by a major international shipping company. It also announced a contract worth approximately €5 million to supply its MoorMaster automated mooring technology to Jawaharlal Nehru Port in India. Delivery is scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2027. In addition, Cavotec signed an exclusive distribution agreement with EVIAS to introduce automatic ground-based charging technology to ports worldwide. The technology is intended to support the electrification of vehicles used in port operations. These contracts had been announced earlier in the quarter and contributed to the company’s wider portfolio of maritime and port electrification projects. However, Cavotec also reported increasing competition in shipboard shore power equipment, which is putting pressure on profit margins. Cost reductions remain a priority For the first nine months of 2026, Cavotec’s revenue increased by 9% to €120.1 million, while order intake rose by 42.2% to €155.9 million. Despite the higher sales and order volumes, the company recorded an EBIT loss of €4.2 million for the nine-month period, compared with a loss of €0.5 million a year earlier. Its net loss widened to €8.9 million from €3.1 million. Cavotec continues to implement cost-saving measures aimed at reducing annual operating costs by approximately €3 million, with the full effect expected by early 2027. The measures generated approximately €0.7 million in savings during the first nine months of 2026, while restructuring costs reached around €1.4 million. David Pagels, CEO of Cavotec, said the company was benefiting from stronger demand and a record order backlog, although profitability remained below expectations. The company expects its ongoing efficiency measures, together with demand for port electrification and automation, to support its longer-term financial performance. Cavotec is scheduled to publish its fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results on 19 February 2027.

REUTERS/Loren Elliott By Vallari Srivastava and Sumit Saha Nov 6 (Reuters) – The Iran conflict has sent tanker rates soaring, forcing sellers to deepen discounts on heavy crude grades and giving US Gulf Coast refiners a cost advantage over Asian rivals, executives said after reporting bumper third-quarter profits. Security threats around the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime chokepoint through which about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies passed before the war started, have disrupted tanker traffic, while higher war-risk insurance premiums and longer voyages have driven upshipping costs. The disruption particularly benefited US Gulf Coast refiners, which could buy discounted heavy crude produced closer to home, including from Canada and Venezuela, while Asian rivals faced sharply higher freight and insurance costs to import similar grades through longer and riskiershipping routes. US refining margins more than doubled in the third quarter. Rising freight costs have widened discounts on Canadian heavy crude, including Western Canadian Select (WCS), which typically trades below US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI), creating a windfall for Gulf Coast refiners, as more than 70% of their facilities are configured to process heavier crude. “The main story right now in the market is freight rates,” Randy Hawkins, vice president of Crude And Feedstocks Supply And Trading at Valero Energy VLO.N, said on a post-earnings conference call. Freight costs for shipping crude from the US Gulf Coast to Asia have jumped to $30-$35 a barrel from about $5 a year earlier, Hawkins said. “Higher freight rates actually give us an advantage into the typical export markets into Latin America,” said Gary Simmons, chief operating officer of Valero, adding that it mainly competes with European barrels in that market. Ample heavy crude supplies from Canada and Venezuela , combined with elevated freight rates, have widened the WTI-WCS differential, lowering feedstock costs, US refining executives said. For Phillips 66 PSX.N, every $1 widening in the WCS-WTI differential is worth about $140 million in gains, Brian Mandell, executive vice president of marketing and commercial, said. Higher shipping costs have also been more than offset by stronger fuel margins, said Delia He, an oil and tanker market analyst at Arrow Shipping. “For every extra dollar of freight, the diesel margin has grown by at least eight,” He said. POSITIONED FOR A STRONG 2027 US refiners have also been shielded from the impacts of higher spot tanker rates following the war due to their advance shipping arrangements. Phillips 66 said it had secured more than 40 time-charter vessels before the Iran conflict , covering about 40% of its asset-based shipping needs. Valero, PBF, Marathon and Canada’s Suncor SU.TO also secured chartered fleets before the war began, insulating them from the surge in prices. Wider differentials are expected to continue to lend strength next year as well, some industry executives said. Top US refiner Marathon Petroleum MPC.N expects record Canadian heavy crude processing in the fourth quarter, while CEO Maryann Mannen has said that margins are expected to remain elevated through at least mid-2027. “In the near term we will take advantage of it,” HF Sinclair DINO.N said of the wider discounts, adding, “we do see the differentials stay wider than they have throughout the near term, at least through 2027.” (Reporting by Vallari Srivastava and Sumit Saha in Bengaluru; Editing by Liz Hampton and Shinjini Ganguli) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. articles.title: Tanker Fleet Growth Threatens Freight Boom, Bullish Secondhand Markets: Analysts
articles.summary: A wave of tanker deliveries is set to test whether geopolitical disruption and longer trading routes can continue supporting charter rates and ship values, according to S&P Global Energy CERA’s latest fleet outlook, after an extraordinary freight market rally pushed some secondhand ship values above newbuilding order...
articles.body: Tanker Fleet Growth Threatens Freight Boom, Bullish Secondhand Markets: Analysts in International Shipping News 07/11/2026 A wave of tanker deliveries is set to test whether geopolitical disruption and longer trading routes can continue supporting charter rates and ship values, according to S&P Global Energy CERA’s latest fleet outlook, after an extraordinary freight market rally pushed some secondhand ship values above newbuilding order prices. Taking newbuild order books and scrapping into account, CERA analysts forecast global tanker capacity will rise from 703.72 million deadweight tons at the end of 2025 to 743.56 million dwt in 2026, 778.35 million dwt in 2027 and 830.61 million dwt in 2028, before reaching 862.98 million dwt in 2029. That would represent cumulative growth of 22.6% over four years. “The tanker market is entering a transition from scarcity-led strength to a period in which demand must work much harder to absorb supply,” according to the fleet outlook published on Oct. 28. “The critical issue is not whether supply will grow, it clearly will, but whether ton-mile demand, scrapping, sanctions-related inefficiencies and operational segmentation can absorb that growth without a material decline in utilization and freight rates.” Record rates Tanker rates across segments have risen to record levels following the outbreak of the US-Iran war at the end of February, boosted by increased ship requirements as Asian importers seek barrels from farther afield and Middle Eastern producers rely on ship-to-ship transfers to mitigate transit risks around the Strait of Hormuz. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the its Global Dirty Tanker Index for non-scrubber-fitted, non-eco tonnage at $840,921.58/day on Nov. 2, compared with $161,876.1/d on Feb. 27, increasing more than 400%. Meanwhile, the Platts Global Clean Tanker Index for non-scrubber-fitted, non-eco tonnage has risen to $143,454.09/d from $38,131.69/d over the same period, increasing more than 275%. The inefficiencies “cannot be assumed to expand indefinitely,” CERA analysts said, while adding that normalizing geopolitical trade patterns, easing sanctions or the return of restricted ships to mainstream employment could increase effective supply more rapidly than the headline fleet figures indicate. Newbuild deliveries The order book comprised 1,494 tankers totaling 184.10 million dwt at the end of September, equivalent to 18.3% of the fleet by ship count but 25.1% by carrying capacity, according to CERA data. Very Large Crude Carriers and Suezmaxes accounted for about 70.5% of ordered capacity. VLCC capacity is forecast to increase 31.5% from 273.31 million dwt in 2025 to 359.28 million dwt in 2029, while Suezmax capacity is projected to expand 30.6% to 143.13 million dwt, the data shows. Product tanker deliveries are more front-loaded, with Aframax/Long Range 2 and Medium Range growth expected to moderate after 2026-2027. “The more challenging period is 2028-29, when VLCC and Suezmax deliveries become exceptionally large,” CERA analysts said. The freight boom has transformed tanker asset markets. CERA estimated a five-year-old VLCC at $185 million, up 57.4% over nine months and around $40 million above a newbuilding order price of $145 million. The analysts described the VLCC market as displaying “one of the clearest inverted asset-value structures in modern shipping history,” as ships in operation can capture record earnings immediately. Ship values XClusiv Shipbrokers assessed October newbuilding prices at $131.5 million for a VLCC, $90.5 million for a Suezmax, $78 million for an Aframax and $52.5 million for an MR2, 4%, 5%, 8% and 8% higher year on year, respectively. Its secondhand estimates showed sharper increases, including a 10-year-old VLCC at $186 million, up 117% year on year, and a 15-year-old VLCC at $160.4 million, up 178%. The market was characterized by “selective investment rather than uniform buying appetite,” the Greek brokerage said in a Nov. 2 note. The brokerage recorded 371 tankers offered for sale during September-October against 146 transactions, with VLCCs and Suezmaxes representing 34% of completed deals but less than 8% of offers. The figures suggested buying was “disproportionately concentrated in larger tankers,” potentially reflecting stronger earnings expectations and confidence in crude transportation, while the availability of older tonnage highlighted owners’ willingness to “capitalize on current asset values,” according to XClusiv Shipbrokers. Veson Nautical similarly said five-year-old tanker values were 32% higher on average than in January, with VLCCs up 70% to $196.3 million, according to a Nov. 3 report. With values above pre-2008 highs and “low visibility on future chartering markets,” Veson expected ordering to “calm.” The analytics firm’s outlook indicates that tanker values will decline over the forecast period, particularly in the VLCC and Suezmax segments, as deliveries accumulate. But Veson expects full restoration of Middle East oil flows to remain unlikely before at least mid-2027, potentially prolonging the inefficiencies supporting near-term earnings and values. articles.body: LPG Exports Declined This Year, but USA’s Kept Growing in Hellenic Shipping News 07/11/2026 L PG exports have been declining so far in 2026, apart from the US. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Banchero Costa said that “global LPG (liquified petroleum gas) trade had been growing steadily for four consecutive years, but 2026 has broken the trend. Total seaborne exports of LPG in 2025 increased by +4.8% year-onyear to 154.7 mln tonnes, according to vessel tracking data from LSEG. This follows the +3.4% y-o-y growth recorded in 2024, and the +2.4% y-oy growth in 2023. In Jan-Sep 2026, however, global seaborne LPG exports declined by -11.7% y-o-y to 102.7 mln tonnes. These totals mask significant differences in export volumes from different exporters, as well as in demand from the various importers. In Jan-Sep 2026, LPG exports from the USA increased by a further +6.3% y-o-y to 56.9 mln tonnes, and now account for 55.4% of all global seaborne LPG exports. LPG exports from the GCC, on the other hand, collapsed by -57.0% y-oy in Jan-Sep 2026, to 12.1 mln tonnes, including 3.5 mln t from the UAE, 2.8 mln t from Saudi Arabia, 2.4 mln t from Qatar, 2.2 mln t from Oman, 1.1 mln t from Kuwait. Shipments from the GCC accounted for just 11.8% of global exports in Jan-Sep 2026, down sharply from 24.2% in the same period of 2025. Exports from the EU increased by +5.9% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 4.3 mln t”. Source: Banchero costa According to Banchero Costa, “in terms of imports, the top destination for LPG in Jan-Sep 2026 was still Mainland China, accounting for 18.6% of global imports. Imports to China declined by -28.1% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 18.8 mln tonnes. Imports to the EU declined by -3.3% y-o-y in Jan-Sep 2026 to 16.3 mln t. The EU accounted for 16.0% of global seaborne LPG imports. Volumes into India declined by -26.4% y-o-y to 12.2 mln tonnes. Imports to Japan were essentially unchanged at -0.1% y-o-y at 7.2 mln tonnes in the same period. Imports to South Korea in Jan-Sep 2026 declined -15.5% y-o-y to 5.3 mln t. Let’s now focus on the United States, which is now the largest exporter of LPG in the world, accounting for 55.4% of global volumes in Jan-Sep 2026”. “As already mentioned above, LPG exports from the USA in Jan-Sep 2026 increased by +6.3% y-o-y to 56.9 mln tonnes. This followed a +6.1% y-o-y increase in 2025, a +11.1% y-o-y increase in 2024, and a +15.0% y-o-y increase in 2023. Top LPG loading ports in the United States in Jan-Sep 2026 were: Houston (24.4 mln t in Jan-Sep 2026), Beaumont (16.2 mln t), Freeport (6.9 mln t), Marcus Hook (5.1 mln t), Corpus Christi (1.6 mln t), Ferndale (1.1 mln t), Geismar (0.5 mln t), Paulsboro (0.3 mln t). 79.6% of volumes in Jan-Sep 2026 were loaded on VLGCs (70+ cu.m.), with 4.8% on LGCs (25-70k cu.m.), 11.2% on MGCs (13-25k cu.m.), and 4.3% on SGCs (0-13k cu.m.). Surprisingly, given the ongoing political tensions, the major destination of American LPG is still Mainland China. Mainland China accounted for 16.4% of the USA’s total seaborne LPG exports in Jan-Sep 2026, well down from the 29.5% peak of 2024. Volumes on this route went through the roof in the first half of the decade, but have corrected sharply since”, the shipbroker said. It added that “whilst LPG trade from the USA to China grounded to a halt in 2019 (it was just 0.3 mln tonnes!), already in 2020 the United States emerged as the number one supplier of LPG to China with 6.2 mln tonnes. This went up to 6.9 mln t in 2021 (+11.9% y-o-y), 9.2 mln t in 2022 (+32.7% y-o-y), 16.3 mln t in 2023 (+77.2% y-o-y), and a peak of 19.7 mln t in 2024 (+20.5% y-o-y). In 2025, however, volumes from the USA to China fell by -39.9% y-o-y to 11.8 mln t, and in Jan-Sep 2026 they declined by a further -7.2% y-o-y to 9.3 mln t. In second place is the European Union, which accounted for 12.0% of USA LPG exports in Jan-Sep 2026. In Jan-Sep 2026, the USA exported 6.8 mln tonnes of LPG to the EU, down -13.7% y-o-y. This followed a +24.8% y-o-y increase in 2025, and a +20.7% y-o-y increase in 2024. The USA also exported 6.8 mln t to Japan in Jan-Sep 2026, up +17.8% yo-y, and 4.8 mln t to South Korea, down -14.3% y-o-y. Shipments to India surged by +282.1% y-o-y to 4.7 mln tonnes, whilst volumes to Indonesia rose by +20.8% y-o-y to 4.4 mln t”, Banchero Costa concluded. However, the bigger story is whether greater fuel flexibility will change how dry bulk ships compete for cargo in the years ahead. Why are some dry bulk owners investing in vessels that can use methanol/ethanol when the usage remains limited? Will the additional investment provide a commercial advantage, or will efficient conventional vessels remain more competitive? Could fuel capability eventually influence which ships charterers prefer? These questions have become more relevant. Although the first methanol/ethanol-capable dry bulk vessels entered the orderbook in 2023, they gained popularity from May 2026, and the number increased to 19 vessels by September. The wider trend is equally interesting. LNG accounted for most of the alternative-fuel vessels in the dry bulk orderbook four years ago. Subsequently, methanol gained ground in 2023, and ammonia came into the picture in 2024. This distinction matters because shipowners still face uncertainty over which alternative fuel will offer the best combination of price, availability and regulatory benefits. Some owners and charterers are addressing this unpredictability through fuel-flexible newbuildings. The 19 methanol/ethanol-capable vessels currently in the dry bulk orderbook are linked to Vale’s move towards fuel-flexible ore carriers, with multiple shipowners ordering these vessels against long-term employment with the miner. Vale’s wider programme involves up to 30 large ore carriers capable of using methanol or ethanol. Others shipowners continue to favour efficient conventional vessels. Pacific Basin replaced four planned methanol dual-fuel Ultramax newbuildings with conventionally fuelled vessels. The change reduced the reported programme cost from $186 million to $156.8 million, although the company retained options for two dual-fuel vessels. The company partly attributed the decision to uncertainty surrounding the IMO Net-Zero Framework. The decision highlights the trade-off between paying more for future fuel flexibility and investing in efficient conventional tonnage today. Owners could also use retrofits to delay that decision. Jayendu Krishna, Head of Maritime Advisory at Drewry and also part of Drewry’s Energy Transition Advisory team, recently highlighted that shipowners have increased methanol retrofit activity as engine manufacturers have developed conversion packages. However, high fuel prices and limited availability continue to constrain actual methanol consumption. The gap between vessel capability and fuel use remains wide. Drewry’s analysis of IMO data shows that alternative fuels met 9.5% of shipping’s energy demand in 2025, but methanol contributed only 0.3% of alternative-fuel consumption. Therefore, building more capable vessels will not drive the transition. Fuel prices, infrastructure, regulation and charterer requirements will determine how owners actually operate these vessels. Recent developments show that ethanol use is moving beyond trials. In October 2026, the methanol dual-fuel containership Maersk Halifax bunkered around 5,000 tonnes of certified bioethanol in Singapore. These factors could impact dry bulk shipping. Unlike containerships, bulk carriers frequently move between regions, which makes widespread fuel availability vital. Owners will have less incentive to use alternative fuels if doing so limits trading flexibility or increases voyage costs. However, the equation could change. If prices of alternative fuels soften, bunkering networks expand, and carbon costs increase the cost of conventional fuels, fuel-flexible vessels could gain an advantage. Major cargo owners could also influence this shift if they increasingly include fuel capability and emissions in chartering decisions as they seek to reduce their Scope 3 emissions. This would affect more than newbuilding choices. It could alter vessels that can compete effectively on a particular route, even if total fleet capacity remains unchanged, thereby changing effective supply. Two vessels may offer similar carrying capacity, but they may not compete equally for the same cargo if their fuel costs, emissions and regulatory exposure differ. Fuel-flexible and more efficient ships could gain access to a wider range of employment, while older conventional vessels may increasingly compete on trades where fuel capability and carbon costs have less influence. Conclusion Nineteen methanol/ethanol-capable vessels on the orderbook do not signal a rapid shift towards ethanol. Instead, it shows that some owners have started paying for flexibility while the industry still lacks clarity on future fuel economics and regulations. The next few years will be crucial and determine whether that flexibility translates into a commercial advantage. Lower alternative-fuel prices, wider bunkering availability, stronger carbon pricing, greater regulatory certainty and greater charterer preference for lower-emission vessels could increase the competitiveness of fuel-flexible ships. If these factors strengthen, fuel capability could increasingly influence chartering, asset values and newbuilding decisions. For dry bulk shipping, this could ultimately create greater differentiation within the fleet. The transition may not immediately change the number of ships available, but it could change which ships compete most effectively for cargo and therefore the effective supply available to different trades. articles.body: Tired of manual, repetitive work that leaves too little time to do business and create value? in International Shipping News 07/11/2026 Shipping has never been a slow-moving business. Vessels move. Markets move. Customers call. Ports become congested. Bunker prices change. New opportunities appear. Risks develop. Decisions often need to be made quickly. Yet many maritime professionals still spend a surprisingly large part of their working day searching for information, checking different systems, copying data into spreadsheets, updating colleagues and digging through emails. People are hired for their experience, relationships and judgment. Not to spend their days searching for vessel information, copying data between systems or trying to figure out which spreadsheet contains the latest update. And that is why manual, repetitive work is not simply an operational inconvenience. It can also have a pretty high commercial cost, because the biggest cost of fragmented software and manual work may be the business you never had time to do or the information you didn’t pursue. When information is scattered across emails, spreadsheets, documents and different software solutions, even relatively simple questions can require several steps. The real cost is therefore not simply the minutes spent searching. It can be: The opportunity you didn’t see. The customer you didn’t call. The decision you made too late. The business you missed. Maritime software should reduce work, not create more of it Over the years, companies involved in maritime business have added more and more software. One for AIS. Another for sea routing. Another for technical descriptions of vessels. Spreadsheets for internal data. Email for communication. SharePoint folders for documents. MS Teams for collaboration. Individually, these tools may solve specific problems. But you need time to find the information, and collectively, they can create another problem: fragmentation, where the knowledge and experience of employees become the integration layer. People have to move between systems, connect the information themselves, remember what needs to happen next, make notes on the side, or copy and paste (or script) information into Excel to try to make sense of it. We believe software should work differently. That thinking is behind ShipIntel Essentials. ShipIntel brings essential maritime features and high-quality real-time and historical AIS data together in one solution, while allowing teams to integrate their own private data and collaborate. From searching for information to having information connected ShipIntel is an interesting alternative to the traditional approach of buying several separate maritime software solutions or developing internal software. Its main proposition is not just vessel tracking or maritime analytics, but combining maritime intelligence, everyday workflows, team collaboration, and private company data in one environment. Imagine looking at a vessel, port, or company and having much of the information you need connected to it. In ShipIntel, a vessel page can combine real-time AIS information, current and previous voyage information, historical trading patterns, ownership, insurance and classification information, sanctions, compliance features, technical descriptions, and historical operational events. On the port page, you will find which vessels and types of vessels have visited each port, how many have visited, which vessels are currently at the anchorages and where they came from, which vessels recently departed and where they are heading. You will also find bunker grades and prices, holidays, local time, weather forecasts, etc. Your team can also connect and add private information to vessels, ports, and companies, including documents, photos, shared notes, and email correspondence. Relevant companies and contacts can also be connected to vessels and ports, ensuring all relevant information is easily accessible in one place. That changes the workflow, broadens your understanding, and hopefully gives you more time to do business. Since people are hired for their experience, relationships, and judgment rather than collecting, categorizing, and cleaning data, it also makes work more enjoyable. Don’t spend your day looking for changes. Let the relevant changes come to you. A lot of manual work in shipping is not really productive work. It is checking information. Has the vessel departed? Has its ETA changed? Which port is the vessel heading to? Has the AIS transponder been turned off? Has the vessel changed destination or reduced its speed? Has the vessel crossed the war risk area we monitor? Why should a person repeatedly check something that software can monitor? ShipIntel allows users to create alerts for vessels, ports, and areas. Notifications can be delivered via email, Microsoft Teams, pop-ups, and mobile devices. Email is another area where maritime professionals spend enormous amounts of working attention The problem is not email itself. The problem is that commercially valuable information often remains buried inside messages. ShipIntel approaches email differently. Instead of creating a standalone email client, ShipIntel connects email with maritime entities and workflows. Emails can be connected to vessels, ports, cargoes, companies, contacts, calculations, fixtures, schedules, and voyages. So rather than searching through an inbox to reconstruct what happened around a vessel or port, the correspondence can become part of the relevant maritime context. Build the vessel lists you actually need Commercial shipping teams rarely need information about every vessel at the same time. They need the right vessels for the situations and purposes they are working on. ShipIntel lets users create vessel lists using criteria including technical characteristics, ownership, classification, P&I insurance, and sanctions. Dynamic lists can automatically update when vessels meet or no longer meet the criteria selected by the user. That can turn another repetitive process into continuous monitoring. Instead of rebuilding the same market picture every morning, teams can create the view they need and monitor changes. Route, compare, and calculate without starting again somewhere else Finding a vessel is often only the beginning. You have to understand routing alternatives, distances, voyage duration, bunker options, or emissions. ShipIntel’s sea-route calculator can route from ports, live vessel AIS positions, or map coordinates. Users can compare alternative routes, account for canal and strait constraints, identify bunker ports along a route, and calculate EU ETS-related carbon emissions. Again, the idea is not simply to add another feature: it is to avoid manual work. Combine maritime intelligence with your company’s own knowledge Public maritime data is valuable. But for most companies, the real competitive advantage appears when external information is combined with what your company knows. Your notes. Your documents. Your contacts. Your correspondence. Your vessel knowledge. Your commercial history. ShipIntel allows proprietary information to be integrated alongside its maritime data while keeping that private information confidential. Teams can attach documents and photos, share notes, and connect correspondence, companies, and contacts to vessels and ports. And because ShipIntel integrates with Microsoft 365, it can work with Microsoft Entra for access control, Exchange for email, SharePoint for accessing information linked to vessels, ports, and companies, and MS Teams for notifications and notes. This matters because digitalization should not mean forcing employees into yet another fragmented silo. The goal should be to connect the information they already use with the maritime intelligence they need. AI changes the equation again There is an even bigger reason why reducing fragmentation matters: AI needs context. If your relevant information remains scattered across spreadsheets, email inboxes, documents, and disconnected software systems, it becomes harder to turn that information into useful intelligence. ShipIntel has therefore been designed as an integrated environment where maritime data can be combined with workflows and proprietary company information. Maritime Optima’s approach is to break down data silos so that richer context can support analysis and AI-enabled outputs. The future of maritime software should therefore not simply be about digitizing today’s manual processes. It should be about removing unnecessary processes altogether. Work smarter with ShipIntel We don’t believe experienced maritime professionals should spend their days copying information between systems. We don’t believe they should repeatedly check information that software can monitor. And we definitely don’t believe valuable commercial knowledge should disappear inside inboxes, spreadsheets, and disconnected applications. People should spend their time where they create the greatest value: Talking to customers. Evaluating opportunities. Understanding markets. Managing risk. Negotiating business. Making decisions. Technology should take care of more of the searching, structuring, connecting, and monitoring. That is the idea behind ShipIntel Essentials: bringing maritime intelligence, workflows, collaboration, and company information closer together in one maritime workspace. Because ultimately, productivity is not about doing more administrative work faster. It is about having more time to do business. Why do companies choose ShipIntel? Save time and development costs ShipIntel by Maritime Optima helps our company reduce the costs and time associated with developing and maintaining software. ShipIntel is a SaaS solution continuously developed and maintained by Maritime Optima without putting the invoice on our desk. Influence future product development ShipIntel gives our employees the opportunity to contribute to the development of software that helps us do more business and that our employees want to use, without us carrying the costs and risks of developing and maintaining it. All product development and improvements are included in the annual fee per seat we pay to Maritime Optima. Get support from real people With an almost 24/7 support channel with a human in the loop, Maritime Optima always wants to help our employees by answering questions and providing guidance when needed. Instead of sending support tickets that might not be answered until the following month, Maritime Optima replies almost immediately. Build on high-quality maritime data and unlock the value of AI ShipIntel helps us tap into a solid foundation of high-quality maritime data and become ready for the potential value that AI can unlock for us. For many years, Maritime Optima has collected, and continues to collect, live raw AIS data from satellites, terrestrial and dynamic AIS sources, along with other publicly available maritime data. They have also used these datasets to train their text-parsing models. Since Maritime Optima cleans, unifies, and processes all these data sources in-house and has trained AI models to understand shipping and specific niches of the shipping industry, we also learn how to work with AI models and our private unstructured data. Maritime Optima has built a very advanced maritime sea routing engine with vessel-specific routing intelligence and constraint-based optimization, which is also available through a separate API. articles.title: Ports face defining decade in fuel transition
articles.summary: The global race to decarbonise shipping is fast becoming a race to prepare ports, according to Lloyd’s Register’s latest Fuel for Thought: Ports report. While shipowners continue to order alternative-fuel vessels at record pace, port infrastructure, safety frameworks and bunkering capabilities are struggling to keep...
articles.body: Ports face defining decade in fuel transition in International Shipping News , Port News 07/11/2026 T he global race to decarbonise shipping is fast becoming a race to prepare ports, according to Lloyd’s Register’s latest Fuel for Thought: Ports report. While shipowners continue to order alternative-fuel vessels at record pace, port infrastructure, safety frameworks and bunkering capabilities are struggling to keep up, creating what LR describes as one of the defining strategic challenges facing the industry this decade. In the report’s foreword, Kamran Ul Haq, senior vice president of LR Ports Advisory, noted that the shipping industry’s fuel transition is already underway, but warned that vessel demand and supply chain readiness are progressing at very different speeds. “That gap creates both risk and opportunity,” Ul Haq said. “Ports that wait for certainty risk falling behind competitors that are already building safety frameworks, licensing regimes and partnerships. Ports that invest too early risk assets that are never fully used.” The report notes that readiness is determined long before the first vessel arrives. According to LR, successful alternative-fuel operations are built on risk assessment, regulation, workforce training and collaboration among port authorities, shipowners, fuel suppliers, emergency services and classification societies. “No port needs to prepare for every fuel at once,” Ul Haq said. “Every port does need a plan.” The report spoke of a rapidly evolving but highly uneven market. LNG remains the most mature alternative fuel, supported by a near-global bunkering network. Methanol has entered commercial use but remains available at only a limited number of major hubs. Ammonia has crossed an important threshold with a first commercial bunkering operation, although adoption remains embryonic, while hydrogen continues to be largely confined to demonstration projects and short-sea applications. Nuclear propulsion, meanwhile, presents an entirely different challenge centred on port access, licensing and liability rather than fuel supply. Vessels vs ports One of the report’s conclusions is that vessel ordering is running significantly ahead of port investment. LR’s analysis identified 1,942 alternative-fuel-capable vessels on order as of January 2026, including 1,259 LNG-capable ships and 385 methanol-capable vessels. By comparison, only 25 ports were actively offering methanol bunkering. “The vessel side of the transition is further advanced than the shore side,” the report noted. The challenge is particularly acute for ammonia and hydrogen. Owners ordering methanol-fuelled vessels join a growing cohort of operators supported by an expanding supply network. Those investing in ammonia- and hydrogen-capable ships face a far less mature infrastructure landscape. The report highlights the growing commercial progress of methanol. Singapore began licensing methanol suppliers from January 2026, while Shanghai recorded a single biomethanol transfer of 8,016 tonnes in August 2026. New international standards have also emerged, including ISO 22120:2026, the first international specification covering methanol bunkering. Yet the report argues that the real challenge is increasingly not bunkering technology but fuel supply. Across the industry, announced low-carbon methanol production capacity stands at 61.8 million tonnes by 2031 but expected operational renewable capacity is only six to 12 million tonnes. As a result, the bottleneck has shifted upstream. For ports, the report warns, the critical issue is often the “last mile” between fuel production and delivery to ships. Bunker vessels, emergency cover, berth access and licensing frameworks all impose costs long before sufficient vessel traffic exists to generate sustainable returns. The report’s notes that there is no single global pathway emerging for port readiness. Instead, different regions and individual ports are pursuing distinct strategies based on local priorities, trade patterns and risk tolerance. “The evidence in this report points to a differentiated picture rather than a single verdict,” LR said. Different choices Within Europe, Rotterdam, Antwerp-Bruges and Hamburg have developed broad multi-fuel programmes, while the Strait of Gibraltar has focused on LNG and bio-LNG. In North Asia, Shanghai has concentrated on LNG, methanol and biofuels, while Ulsan has emerged as the pioneer in ammonia bunkering. According to the report, “individual port authorities’ strategic choices, not simply geography, do most of the explanatory work”. LR identifies LNG as the clear leader in infrastructure maturity. Existing LNG networks also provide a foundation for future bio-LNG and e-methane deployment. Methanol is progressing rapidly because its ambient-temperature handling characteristics allow ports to reuse much of their existing liquid-fuel infrastructure. The scale-up has been dramatic, with single methanol transfers increasing from 475 tonnes at Antwerp-Bruges in 2023 to 8,016 tonnes in Shanghai in 2026. “LNG already has the network, and bio-LNG and e-methane can largely inherit it,” the report says. “Methanol has separated itself from ammonia and hydrogen in commercial maturity.” Ammonia’s progress, by contrast, remains cautious and heavily dependent on safety governance. Ulsan remains the only port identified in the report as having completed commercial ammonia bunkering. Other leading ports, including Rotterdam and Singapore, remain in pilot or trial phases, while Hamburg’s physical ammonia supply infrastructure is not expected before 2029. Hydrogen faces even greater challenges. LR concludes that it “remains, realistically, a short-sea and harbour-craft fuel for the foreseeable future”, despite regulatory progress. Biofuel blends, meanwhile, continue to offer the most immediate and practical compliance route for many operators because they can use established supply chains and infrastructure. The report also highlights growing interest in nuclear propulsion. However, LR emphasises that nuclear-powered vessels will require specialised licensing, security and liability frameworks rather than conventional bunkering infrastructure. Projects involving Long Beach, Corpus Christi, Rotterdam, Charleston and Felixstowe are exploring those questions. For shipowners and charterers, the report argues that fuel strategy can no longer be separated from trading patterns: “Fuel choice and trade route are now inseparable… Any newbuild or conversion decision should be stress-tested against the specific ports a vessel will call at, not against the industry’s aggregate progress.” The report points to green shipping corridors as one of the clearest indicators of where reliable alternative-fuel supply will emerge first. It also identifies biofuel blends as “the lowest-risk, highest-availability compliance option for owners who need to act now”. articles.summary: The list of successful alternative-fuel bunker operations keeps growing, as seen over the past week. articles.body: The Week in Alt Fuels: Ammonia and methanol bunkering gain ground in International Shipping News 07/11/2026 The list of successful alternative-fuel bunker operations keeps growing, as seen over the past week. Two ammonia-capable vessels received green ammonia in different parts of the world. In South Korea, Eastern Pacific Shipping’s Terra Clove was bunkered at Ulsan. The fuel came from Envision Energy’s production facility in Inner Mongolia and was delivered by South Korean supplier Lotte Fine Chemical. CMB.TECH’s Mineral Europa was bunkered with an unspecified quantity of green ammonia in a ship-to-ship bunker operation at Australia’s Port Hedland. The fuel was delivered by the ammonia bunker vessel Shenghang Yongle in a trial that the port authority said builds on its 2024 ship-to-ship ammonia transfer pilot. In China, OOCL’s methanol-capable container ship OOCL Grace received 983 mt of bio-methanol at Yantian. These operations demonstrate that alternative fuels can move through diverse supply chains and into ships’ bunker tanks. But making such deliveries routine is another matter. Some ports are now looking at ways to build more consistent demand rather than relying on individual bunker stems. Singapore and Qingdao, for instance, have laid the groundwork for more methanol bunkering along their shared shipping corridor. Singapore’s port authority and Qingdao Port will also explore ways to pool methanol bunker demand between the ports. Aggregating demand could help suppliers justify regular deliveries and investment in bunker and storage infrastructure, even if the two sides have yet to disclose a timeline for the proposed pilots. The potential scale of future demand is becoming clearer too. A feasibility study by the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach estimates that methanol bunker demand at the two ports could be 64,000-250,000 mt/year by 2030. LNG demand could be 65,000-115,000 mt/year, the study added. Those figures offer a glimpse of the market that bunker suppliers may need to serve. But demand forecasts are only one side of the equation. Availability of bunker infrastructure remains another important consideration. For instance, only 29 ports worldwide offered some type of methanol bunkering in April, according to Clarksons Research data cited in a report by the Global Maritime Forum and University College London. Availability of ammonia bunkering is even more limited, with only a handful of major ports having conducted ammonia bunker operations. In comparison, DNV counts 171 methanol- and ethanol-capable vessels in operation and another 292 on order for delivery through 2031. It counts eight ammonia-capable vessels in operation and 42 on order for delivery by 2030. More ports around the world are gaining practical experience with alternative-fuel bunkering. But turning these individual operations into regular commercial deliveries and wider fuel uptake will require sufficient fuel availability, storage capacity and supporting infrastructure. In other alt fuels news this week, DNV recorded 53 alternative-fuel vessel orders in October, 30 of them LNG-capable. Four ammonia-capable vessels were also ordered, ending a two-month spell without new orders for the fuel. Japanese marine engine maker Japan Engine Corporation has won an order for four 60-bore ammonia-capable main engines, one for each car carrier in a project that seven Japanese companies announced on 27 October. The car carriers, due in 2030, are expected to be supplied by a planned ammonia bunker vessel. Denmark’s European Energy has partnered with Canadian ethanol producer Greenfield Global to develop a plant in Québec that could produce up to 48,000 mt/year of e-methanol. The companies are targeting ships as one of the potential users of the fuel, European Energy said. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/ 2026-11-07 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: GMS Week 45 – Bids Hold Fast Against the Tide in Weekly Demolition Reports 07/11/2026 Last week’s improving recycling sentiment has encountered a changing international backdrop. Crude oil has retreated sharply, domestic steel prices have weakened across several destinations, and freight continues to fluctuate. Yet recycling indications remain unchanged across all four markets. Buying appetite remains healthy, particularly in Bangladesh, although the persistent shortage of available candidates continues to prevent stronger sentiment from translating into fresh transactions. Oil supplied the week’s most striking movement. Brent retreated towards USD 99 per barrel on Friday, while WTI traded around USD 91, reversing much of last week’s advance. Expectations of easing Middle Eastern tensions encouraged the correction, although renewed security incidents in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz demonstrated that shipping risks remain unresolved. Lower crude may ease operating expenses, but uncertainty surrounding regional passage continues to influence tanker employment and owners’ recycling decisions. Dry freight offered mixed signals. The Baltic Dry Index recovered to 2,740 on Thursday, November 5, from 2,712 a week earlier, having fallen to 2,590 during the intervening sessions. Capesizes strengthened to 4,191 and Panamaxes improved to 1,956, while Supramaxes eased to 1,824. The uneven recovery continues to provide ageing vessels with trading alternatives, restricting the supply of recycling candidates. Steel markets moved against recyclers. Indian plate declined considerably during the week, while Pakistan recorded a further correction and Chinese steel continued to soften. Bangladesh remained unchanged, although a strengthening Dollar placed additional pressure on the Taka amid substantial foreign currency requirements for energy imports. Weaker steel realisations are restricting purchasing flexibility, even as recycling price indications remain unchanged. India also faced an important regulatory hurdle. On November 4, the European Parliament’s ENVI Committee voted to object to the proposed inclusion of Indian ship recycling yards on the European approved list, citing environmental concerns over beaching methods. The objection is not a final rejection. A full parliamentary vote is expected later this month, while the final binding decision remains subject to EU Member State approval. The development introduces uncertainty into Alang’s expanding compliance ambitions. At the beaches, Bangladesh continues to demonstrate the strongest conventional buying appetite, supported by expectations of improving seasonal demand. Pakistan remains static amid limited fresh supply, while India continues to pursue opportunities in specialist and higher-value vessels. Turkey maintains its selective approach. Physical activity nevertheless continued, with a sizeable tanker arriving at Chattogram, additional tonnage reaching Alang and a previously secured bulker completing delivery at Gadani. The overall market remains stable despite softer steel and changing energy conditions. Buyers are maintaining their positions, but freight earnings and second-hand alternatives continue to discourage owners from releasing ageing ships. Bangladesh has the confidence, India retains its specialist strengths, and Pakistan and Turkey remain measured. The bids are holding their ground. The missing ingredient remains a steady supply of willing sellers. For Week 45 of 2026, GMS Market Rankings / Vessel indications are as below. articles.body: COP31: Seas At Risk is calling for urgent action to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) in International Shipping News 07/11/2026 As world leaders gather at COP31, Seas At Risk is calling for urgent action to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) and black carbon emissions to protect marine ecosystems and accelerate a fair transition away from fossil fuels in international shipping. The latest scientific reports, such as the UNEP Emissions Gap Report, deliver a stark warning: exceeding the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming threshold is now inevitable. But how far that temperature rises, and for how long, depends upon governments making the right choices today. The ocean is one of our biggest allies in the fight against climate change. It absorbs around 90% of the excess heat trapped by GHG, helping to regulate the earth’s climate. However, this comes at an enormous cost: rising ocean temperatures, marine heatwaves, acidification and mounting pressure on marine biodiversity. Every fraction of a degree of warming increases these risks. Even if global temperatures return to 1.5 degrees after temporarily exceeding it, some damage to the marine environment could be irreversible. COP31 must be about action, not just ambition. Governments must turn their commitments into real emission reductions, across all sectors, including shipping. • Every fraction of a degree matters and the ocean cannot wait Current climate policies are taking the world towards dangerous levels of warming. Even more ambitious pathways will temporarily exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius and depend upon intensified emission reductions and the uptake of clean fuels and technology. For the ocean, any rise in warming spells danger. Marine ecosystems such as coral reefs, along with polar seas and coastal communities are on the forefront of escalating risks due to rising sea and atmosphere temperatures. Seas At Risk is calling for immediate intensification of efforts to reduce GHG emissions and deep cuts in emissions of methane and black carbon rather than relying on carbon removal which cannot be deployed at scale and must not replace efforts to decarbonise. Seas At Risk is fighting for: -A maritime sector that uptakes clean fuels and technologies such as wind propulsion, -A rapid reduction in super pollutants like methane and black carbon, that is up to 1600 more warming and is destroying the Arctic, -A healthy ocean that fights climate change. It naturally absorbs carbon, protects the coastline, feeds us and stabilises the weather, -Funding, technology and international support for small islands, coastal communities, and low-income nations. • The International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework: a critical opportunity for shipping climate action International shipping cannot wait on the sidelines of global climate action. As we get closer to critical discussions and decisions in December, the International Maritime Organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework would establish global measures to reduce GHG emissions from ships, including a fuel GHG intensity standard and an economic mechanism. Its implementation could help accelerate shipping’s transition towards cleaner energy, improve investment certainty and support international cooperation. Yet the framework, approved by IMO Member States in April 2025, is waiting to be adopted and remains politically contested. Any further delays, or weakening of the framework, beyond the next discussions at the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee would postpone the introduction of global binding measures. Seas At Risk is calling for an ambitious, effective and equitable IMO Net-Zero Framework, that deliver real emission reductions and includes a dedicated fund to support countries and communities facing disproportionate transition costs and the greatest climate impacts. Anais Rios, Senior Shipping Policy Officer, Seas At Risk, says: “Every fraction of a degree of heating risks large-scale and irreversible damage to our ocean and its ecosystems. At COP31, world leaders must turn promise into action and cut fossil fuels from every sector, including shipping, to protect the ocean that protects us from climate change.” Source: Seas At Risk 2026-11-07 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Evos is Europe’s second-largest independent liquid storage operator, with eight port-based terminals across the Netherlands, Germany, Spain, Belgium and Malta. Its portfolio also includes emerging fuels such as sustainable aviation fuel, biofuels, methanol and bioethanol. Adani said the business has maintained average commercial occupancy of 99%, with much of its revenue supported by long-term contracts. The acquisition also gives Adani greater exposure to Europe’s evolving fuel market as demand grows for alternative marine and aviation fuels. Adani Ports, India’s largest private port operator, has been expanding internationally through investments in port infrastructure and logistics. Its existing overseas operations include terminals in Sri Lanka, Israel, Tanzania and Australia. The transaction carries an equity value of €1.18 billion and will be financed through debt, subject to regulatory approvals and works council consultation. MUFG has provided financing commitments of up to €2.8 billion for the proposed transaction. The companies did not announce an expected closing date. REUTERS/Juan Carlos Hernandez The Trump administration has expanded sanctions targeting Cuba’s maritime and energy sectors, identifying five Cuban-flagged vessels as blocked property and opening the door to further sanctions against foreign companies operating in the country’s marine industry. The measures, announced Thursday by the State Department , target eight companies and two individuals accused of supporting the Cuban government through petroleum shipments, offshore business networks and military procurement. The action also includes a new Treasury Department determination allowing sanctions against foreign persons operating in Cuba’s marine, manufacturing, electronics and technology sectors. Among those targeted is Cyprus-based Caroil Transport Marine Ltd., which manages Cuban-flagged tankers involved in transporting energy products. The company was previously sanctioned in 2019 under U.S. measures targeting Venezuela. Three vessels associated with Caroil were identified as blocked property: the crude oil tanker Esperanza , chemical and products tanker Gloria C , and products tanker Maria Cristina . Washington also sanctioned Panama-based Tentacool Commercial Inc., the registered owner of Gloria C , and Cuba-based Internacional Maritima SA, which owns Esperanza . Another Cuban shipping company, Petroleos Maritimos del Caribe S.A. (Petromarca), was designated alongside two vessels it manages: the LPG carrier Emilia and crude oil tanker Lourdes . Three of the five vessels were already listed under earlier Venezuela-related sanctions, while Emilia and Gloria C were newly added. The administration also targeted Guillermo Faustino Rodriguez Lopez Calleja, whom the State Department linked to a network of maritime shipping companies transporting petroleum products to and from Cuba. The sanctions come as Cuba continues to struggle with fuel shortages and electricity outages, making imported energy supplies increasingly important. Under the measures, property belonging to designated entities under U.S. jurisdiction is blocked, and U.S. persons are generally prohibited from conducting business with them. Foreign shipping operators and maritime service providers could also face additional sanctions exposure. The State Department said existing authorizations for humanitarian trade, including food and medicine, remain in place. The latest action adds another layer of restrictions to Cuba’s energy trade, potentially complicating the financing, management and operation of vessels serving the island. articles.title: EU Lawmakers Push Back Against Approval of Indian Ship Recycling Yards
articles.summary: A European Parliament committee has voted to oppose the approval of two Indian ship recycling yards, dealing a setback to shipping industry efforts to expand access to South Asia’s shipbreaking...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network A Maersk Line containership seen alongside other ships a Hong Kong Convention-approved ship recycling facility in Alang, India. Photo credit: Maersk A European Parliament committee has voted to oppose the approval of two Indian ship recycling yards, dealing a setback to shipping industry efforts to expand access to South Asia’s shipbreaking facilities. The Parliament’s Environment Committee voted Wednesday to object to the European Commission’s proposal to add Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in Alang-Sosiya, Gujarat, to the European List of approved ship recycling facilities. The objection passed by 48 votes to 26, with five abstentions, according to European recycling industry association Recycling Europe . The vote comes after months of lobbying by shipping industry groups, environmental organizations, European steelmakers and recyclers over whether Indian facilities using the controversial beaching method should qualify under European environmental rules. The two yards had received preliminary backing from the European Commission following inspections intended to determine whether they meet the requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. Their inclusion would mark the first time Indian ship recycling facilities have been added to the European List. At the center of the dispute is beaching, a method in which ships are driven onto tidal shorelines before being dismantled. Lawmakers opposing the proposal argue that cutting ships apart in intertidal areas makes it difficult to contain oil, heavy metals and other hazardous materials, even at facilities that have invested in improved infrastructure and environmental controls. The objection also raises concerns about downstream waste management, including scrap steel sent to local re-rolling mills that have not been assessed against European industrial emissions standards. The NGO Shipbreaking Platform welcomed the committee vote , arguing that approving the facilities would undermine the environmental protections established under EU law. “Today’s vote in the European Parliament sends a strong political message to the European Commission,” said Ingvild Jenssen, the organization’s executive director. Recycling Europe also welcomed the decision, arguing that approving facilities without conclusive evidence of compliance would place European recyclers at a competitive disadvantage. The opposition follows a coordinated campaign by European steelmakers, recyclers, trade unions and environmental organizations. As gCaptain reported in September , a coalition including EUROFER, IndustriAll Europe, the European Environmental Bureau, Recycling Europe, Transport & Environment and the NGO Shipbreaking Platform urged the Commission to withdraw its proposal. The groups argued that beaching facilities cannot meet European requirements for pollution containment and warned that approving the Indian yards could undermine investments made by European recycling facilities to comply with stricter environmental and worker safety standards. Their concerns extend beyond pollution. The groups also argue that end-of-life ships represent an important source of scrap steel and other secondary raw materials that should be recovered within Europe. Shipping associations have taken the opposite position. In September, BIMCO, European Shipowners | ECSA, the International Chamber of Shipping, INTERCARGO, INTERTANKO and the World Shipping Council welcomed the Commission’s proposal , arguing that approval should be based on individual facilities’ compliance rather than their location or recycling method. The campaign intensified on September 17, when eight shipping organizations, including CLIA and INTERFERRY, sent a joint letter to EU environment and transport ministers urging member states to approve the two yards. The associations argue that the facilities have invested heavily in infrastructure, worker safety and environmental management, and that rejecting yards found compliant through the Commission’s inspection process would undermine the credibility of the EU approval system. Shipping groups also warn that the European List faces a shortage of suitable recycling capacity as more vessels approach the end of their operating lives. European Shipowners | ECSA reiterated that position ahead of Wednesday’s vote. “The inclusion of the two Indian yards in the EU list is a long-awaited and very welcome step, which rewards investments made to meet EU standards,” ECSA Secretary General Sotiris Raptis said in an October 28 statement . The disagreement highlights a broader divide over how the European Union should regulate an industry concentrated largely in South Asia. More than 95% of global ship recycling takes place in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan and Turkey, according to the shipping associations. All four countries are parties to the International Maritime Organization’s Hong Kong Convention, which entered into force on June 26, 2025, establishing international requirements for safe and environmentally sound ship recycling. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation goes further in certain areas. Since December 2018, large EU-flagged commercial vessels have been required to use facilities on the European List, regardless of where those facilities are located. The latest adopted EU list , published in February, contained 41 facilities, including 30 in Europe, 10 in Turkey and one in the United States. Environmental campaigners dispute the shipping industry’s capacity argument, pointing to more than 2 million light displacement tonnes of combined annual capacity at facilities already approved by the EU, which they argue is sufficient to handle recent recycling volumes involving EU-flagged and EU-owned ships. The European Commission itself has acknowledged weaknesses in the existing system, including the practice of shipowners reflagging vessels outside the EU shortly before recycling to avoid the regulation’s requirements. Wednesday’s committee vote does not amount to a final rejection of the Indian yards. The objection, introduced by Green lawmaker Sara Matthieu and supported by representatives from other political groups, is expected to go before the full European Parliament later in November. Even if adopted, it would not legally require the Commission to withdraw its proposal. EU member states will have the final say.
